title: ‘Top priority’: RBA signals more rate hikes needed
full_text:
Bad news folks, the Reserve Bank will be lifting rates at least once more before Christmas.
The outlook for Australian stocks just keeps getting tougher as oil prices march toward $US100 a barrel and inflation worries mount.
On Tuesday, the ASX 200 dived 1 per cent to a six week low of 8920.8 points as the Iran war showed no sign of ending, consumer and business confidence surveys slumped, and RBA assistant governor Sarah Hunter warned of potential need to restart interest rate hikes.
Hunter stressed that the central bank board views elevated inflation as its “top priority” and may need to raise interest rates again to tackle it, even as the property market starts to dive.
“They’ve been pretty clear that they don’t really have tolerance for inflation to continue to be” above target for an extended period, Hunter said at a conference in Sydney.
“If there is a sense that inflation is going to be stronger than we think in the context of our forecast, the board may well have to raise interest rates to tackle that.”
The sharemarket fell further after Westpac joined the call for a restart of interest rate hikes, citing “growing evidence of a more resilient household sector, and a larger-than-expected impetus from a data centre focused investment boom.”
“While the housing sector is playing out weaker than earlier forecast, the outlook for overall growth is now firmer and the tech sector is adding new cost pressures not evident previously,” said Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis, who was an RBA assistant governor.
Tactically, Ellis said the bank’s leadership would strongly favour a November hike over September.
However, the chance of a hike this month is “not zero” and investors should watch RBA communications closely for signs that its leadership is “anxious to move.”
RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser was due to appear on the ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday night.
Market speculation of renewed interest rate hikes ramped up after stronger than expected inflation and economic growth data in recent weeks.
Money market pricing now implies a more than 60 per cent chance of a 25 basis points rate hike this month, at least one rate hike by November and an 80 per cent chance of two rate hikes by March.
But Hunter cautioned that the July inflation data is monthly and can be volatile and RBA officials have made clear they prefer to see quarterly reports when judging the inflation outlook.
The RBA currently expects inflation to the midpoint of its 2-3 per cent target band in early 2028.
A further increase in the cash rate from the current level of 4.35 per cent would hit the highest level in about 15 years. It comes as a national home value index has dropped 3.6 per cent since March.
HSBC recently downgraded its house price forecast to predict a 13 per cent fall in the national average after calling for back to back interest rate hikes from the RBA in September and November.
Asked about the collapse of Sydney residential property developer Bathla Group, which is now in talks with creditors to secure funding after it fell into insolvency with debts of $3.4bn, Hunter said the central bank is monitoring the situation in terms of financial stability risks.
“Private credit has been an area that we’ve paid much more attention to recently,” she said.
“We don’t, at the moment, see systemic signs of stress, so we can’t see that it’s sort of spreading through our banks and everything else. But it’s certainly something that we’ll keep an eye on.”
The administrators of Bathla have stood down hundreds of staff, One Nation's plan to allow Australians early access to their super has been attacked by Labor. Plus, housing affordability in Australia has fallen to an all-time low.
Hunter also discussed monetary policy transmission channels in the housing market, noting that housing turnover is the most immediate, while the wealth effect is relatively small.
“The third channel that we pay a lot of attention to is construction activity,” she said.
“So what does this move in house prices mean for the viability of projects for developers and how does that come through in terms of new dwelling construction.”
Asked about the chance of a recession, she said “that’s not our baseline forecast.”
Surging fuel prices, the prospect of further interest rate hikes and a housing downturn sweeping Australia’s capital cities have driven consumer sentiment back into deeply pessimistic territory.
The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment index shed 5.2 per cent in August, falling to levels last seen following the outbreak of war in Iran, off the back of pump prices lifting back above $2-a-litre and a hot inflation reading stoking fears the RBA may hike rates for a fourth time this year.
Australian business confidence remained well below its long-run average and conditions turned negative for the first time in years last month according to NAB.
The NAB monthly business survey showed confidence fell 2 points to minus 8 points and conditions 5 points to minus 1 point with global uncertainty, jumpy oil prices and cost pressures weighing on the mood of Australian businesses.
The fall in conditions was widespread, hitting most industries, but a 10-point fall in profitability drove much of the decline, alongside a 5-point drop in trading conditions.
